claims.text: Supply is the quantity of a good that producers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price over a period of time.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A producer's willingness to sell counts as supply where the producer is also able to offer the good, with stock, capacity or the right to sell it; a hope to sell without the ability to offer stays outside supply.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Supply is sometimes confused with demand: supply counts the quantities sellers are willing and able to offer at each price, while demand, from topic 2.3, counts the quantities buyers are willing and able to buy; the test is which side of the market the quantity belongs to.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A supply schedule lists the quantities a producer is willing and able to offer at each of a series of prices, and a supply curve draws the same relationship with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, sloping upward from left to right.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The relationship between a good's price and the quantity supplied tends to be positive: as the price rises, the quantity supplied tends to rise, and as the price falls, the quantity supplied tends to fall, because a higher price tends to make producing the good more worthwhile.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Supply is the whole relationship between price and quantity, while quantity supplied is the amount offered at one single price; a change in the good's own price changes quantity supplied and moves the market along the supply curve, while supply itself stays as it was.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A rise in the good's own price causes an extension in supply - a movement up along an unchanged supply curve to a larger quantity offered - and a fall in the price causes a contraction in supply, a movement down the same curve to a smaller quantity offered.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Individual supply is the quantity of a good that one producer is willing and able to offer for sale at each price, and market supply is the quantity that all the producers in a market together are willing and able to offer at that price.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Market supply at each price is found by adding together the quantities that every individual producer offers at that price, working price by price through the schedule; drawn as curves, the market supply curve is the horizontal sum of the individual supply curves.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: If one Oshakati textile firm offers 400 metres of cloth a week at N$25 a metre, a second offers 600 metres at the same price, and the rest of the market together offers 1 500 metres, market supply at N$25 is 2 500 metres a week: 400 + 600 = 1 000 metres, and 1 000 + 1 500 = 2 500 metres.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The conditions of supply are the influences on supply other than the good's own price, including the costs of the inputs used to make the good, the technology of production, indirect taxes and subsidies on the good, the prices of other goods the producer could make instead, the weather for farm and fishing goods, and the number of sellers in the market.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A change in a condition of supply shifts the whole supply curve: an increase in supply shifts the curve to the right, meaning producers offer a larger quantity at every price, and a decrease in supply shifts it to the left, meaning producers offer a smaller quantity at every price.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The test for a movement or a shift of the supply curve is whether the good's own price changed: a change in the good's own price causes a movement along the curve, whereas a change in a condition of supply, with the price unchanged, shifts the whole curve.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A fall in the costs of the inputs used to make a good tends to shift the supply curve to the right, because producing becomes more worthwhile at each price, so producers tend to offer a larger quantity for sale than before.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: If Kaoko Juice raises the price of a bottle from N$8 to N$12 and, at the higher price, offers 900 bottles a week instead of 600, the change is an extension in supply of 300 bottles a week, since 900 - 600 = 300 bottles, brought about by the price alone.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: An improvement in technology or productivity lowers the cost of producing each unit and makes production more worthwhile at every price, so supply tends to increase and the supply curve shifts to the right; a fall in productivity tends to shift it left.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: An indirect tax on a good works like an extra cost on each unit, so supply decreases and the supply curve shifts to the left, while a subsidy to producers works like a cost cut, so supply increases and the curve shifts to the right.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Where a producer can switch resources between products, a rise in the price of another good it could make tends to draw resources towards that good, decreasing the supply of the original good at every price; a fall in the other good's price tends to increase it.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Market supply is the sum of what every seller offers at each price, so firms entering a market tend to increase market supply and shift the curve to the right, while firms leaving tend to decrease it and shift the curve to the left.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
